Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others

Vignette:
Tuan was forty-seven when he finally booked the intake appointment, but the weight of it had been building for three years. The summer his eight-year-old son developed a sudden, violent gastrointestinal infection quickly spiraled into septic shock. The private pediatric clinic where they first sought care had missed the early warning signs. By the time his son was stabilized in the ICU, the medical team had administered aggressive intravenous sedation and repeatedly wiped down his son’s infected veins with alcohol swabs. Tuan had watched the cardiac monitors, felt the heavy antiseptic fog in the cramped room, and experienced his own head spinning as he sat on the hard plastic chair, certain that the attending physician and the night-shift nurse had failed him. He had come to believe that their negligence had nearly taken his boy’s life, a conviction that took root and never loosened its grip. In the months that followed, the hospital’s presence in his life shifted from a place of healing to a landscape of dread. When he drove past medical centers, the sharp, antiseptic scent seeping from ventilation grates would hit him before he could look away. Around the same moment, a wave of dizziness would pull at his equilibrium, making the asphalt look uneven. He avoided those blocks altogether, taking longer routes through industrial zones, though the detours only meant he arrived at errands exhausted. The smell of hospital alcohol on a stranger’s hands at the grocery store checkout produced the same disorienting drop in his chest. He would step back, mutter an excuse about needing air, and walk out into the sunlight. He was certain that stepping closer would only invite the same vulnerability he had spent years outrunning. Work as a park ranger offered little reprieve. His station maintained a well-stocked first aid kit for responding to injured hikers, and the periodic mandatory reviews required him to handle the antiseptic wipes and gauze. Each time the chemical tang rose, his vision blurred and his stomach turned over. He began volunteering for trail maintenance and wildlife surveys, deliberately missing the clinical briefings. At home, his marriage strained under the quiet logistics of his avoidance. When his wife, Mai, began bringing up their son’s recent clinic appointments or gently asking how he felt about the recent medication adjustments, his throat closed. He changed the subject, walked to the garage to sand furniture, or simply sat in his truck with the engine off until she stopped asking. The silence between them was not chosen lightly. It was a boundary he had drawn around the memory of the night the monitors flatlined and then rushed back to life. His mind frequently circled back to the medical records, the delayed blood work, the nurse who had logged the wrong dosage. He spent hours rehearsing exactly how he would confront the clinic staff, what he would demand, and how he would make them answer for their carelessness. This was not anger that flared and faded; it was a steady, grinding loop he allowed himself to revisit every evening at the kitchen table, tracing the hypothetical steps until his fingers went numb. He dwelled on what the other people involved had done to him, cataloging their missteps like evidence in a case that would never be tried. What frightened him most was the feeling that the world remained fundamentally unsafe, that the same oversight could strike again without warning. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single breaking point but the accumulated weight of a life narrowing in scope. He caught himself refusing to sit in the passenger seat of any vehicle passing a clinic, noticed he had not spoken to Mai about their son’s recovery in over a year, and realized he could no longer tolerate the antiseptic scent in his own ranger station’s supply closet. He was most afraid of continuing to drift through his days bracing for the next wave of dizziness or the next unasked question, but he hoped, for the first time in three years, that someone might help him untangle the way the past kept colonizing his present.
